Overall Product Owner responsibilities are to:

  1. Verify that the final products provide the most benefit possible to the stakeholders and/or organization as a whole;
  2. Provide guidance in terms of what has to be delivered for each product and in which priority, so that item 1, above, is met.

More specifically, to deliver on the above, the Product Owner is responsible for:

  • Selecting candidate work items for the upcoming sprint during the sprint planning session
  • Answering all questions from the team and providing necessary clarifications about the product
  • Accepting and approving completed work items, or parts of the product
  • Managing and refining the Product Backlog as detailed below
  • Scheduling the sprint review, confirming stakeholder attendance and leading parts of the meeting such as summarizing work completed
  • Deciding when to release the product
  • Coordinating delivery of the final product to the appropriate users

As the sole person responsible for managing the Product Backlog, the Product Owner must also be responsible for:

  • Communicating with the stakeholders to understand their requirements
    Typically, any product has more than one stakeholder, most often a few groups of them. In some cases, the Product Owner may be the key stakeholder. Product Owner is normally the first person to gather and understand the needs of stakeholders and ultimately translates that vision into concrete work items. This way they become the single point of contact between the team and the stakeholders thereby reducing the number of communication lines needed.
  • Maintaining the work to be completed in the Product Backlog to best achieve goals and optimize the value of the work performed
    The Product Owner is responsible for translating the product vision into a number of components of work so that both the value of the product and the work of the team is maximized to achieve the outlined goals. How this is achieved varies across organizations however typically the Product Backlog is used.   

While the above mentioned items are the sole responsibility of the Product Owner, he/she may be supported by the team in order to efficiently carry out these responsibilities.

The Product Owner needs to be available to his or her team(s) to address questions and clarify concerns in a timely manner; the effective management of stakeholders also requires time and effort. Typically, with a moderately complex product and a single team, 30-40% of an individual’s time would be needed to perform the Product Owner role. With more teams the time needed scales (non-linearly), up to 100% of PO's time with 2-8 teams, the precise limit depending on support provided to the PO by the team (e.g., from experienced business analysts) and complexity of the product.

Furthermore the time required from the Product Owner will change depending on:

  • The stage of the project - more time needed at project initiation to prepare the initial Product Backlog
  • Maturity and capability of the team(s)
  • Product ownership experience
  • Familiarity with business and product domain

Ideally, the PO is co-located with the team. If the PO is unable to co-locate with the team or has insufficient availability, another person might play a role of proxy Product Owner. Proxy PO should be in close touch with the PO, and thus be able to convey guidance to the team. This role is beneficial when it helps the team get guidance, such as answers to urgent questions, more quickly. To be successful and effective, proxy PO should have sufficient business acumen and understanding.

The Product Owner role requires an individual with certain skills and characteristics, including:

  • Business knowledge
  • Communication skills
  • Stakeholder management skills 

Business knowledge

Business knowledge is important for the Product Owner because he/she is the decision maker that informs the final product. That means the Product Owner should understand relevant factors, including the market, stakeholders' needs, the business and business strategy in order to make sound decisions. As these are important and time-consuming responsibilities, being adequately committed to the project becomes increasingly crucial.

A business understanding is necessary in order to triangulate stakeholders’ requirements, market situation and other factors. Once the Product Owner has a firm grip on these factors he/she can process them to come up with a consistent vision of the product to be delivered.

Although Product Owner is the final decision maker, they do not need to be an expert on everything. Thus an ability to connect team members with various expert stakeholders is required.

Communication skills

Communication is a large part of the Product Owner's responsibilities, in both written and verbal form. The Product Owner role requires working closely with key stakeholders throughout the organization and beyond, so he or she must be able to clearly and concisely communicate different messages to various stakeholders.

Product Owners need to communicate with the team effectively, so that all the requirements are clear, vision is conveyed and understood, and the team is not blocked by lack of clear direction. Usually the team requires some of the Product Owner’s time throughout the sprint to answer questions, clarify requirements and sign off on completed work.

Stakeholder management skills

Stakeholder management could be described as having the ability to:

  • Understand stakeholders' needs and requirements
  • Gain consensus on product vision among the stakeholders
  • Manage stakeholder expectations
  • Build trust in the group of stakeholders, enabling the Product Owner to guide the team within the given governance framework

The Product Owner typically needs to closely interact with stakeholders so they are normally chosen from within the organization’s relevant domain (and thus have an existing network). Alternatively, a domain expert may become the Product Owner and then build their own network of contacts.

Obtaining consensus on the requirements across an often broad stakeholder group can be challenging. A key skill of the Product Owner is to obtain this consensus so that the team is clear on the objectives. This requires the Product Owner to approach conflict with a solution-focused approach, while maintaining a collaborative mindset to minimize the negative, and mediation skills.

One person is assigned the role of Product Owner. The Product Owner may represent a broader group of stakeholders but only a single individual holds the title and all associated responsibilities.

Seniority is one of the key factors when selecting an effective Product Owner, they require the respect and trust of the organization to set direction when consulting with stakeholders. They also need to be sufficiently available to support the teams. This means that senior individuals may find the role challenging due to their limited availability and will likely need to relinquish certain responsibilities to create sufficient time to be an effective Product Owner. Meanwhile, less senior candidates might struggle to gain access to necessary stakeholders who would provide the mandate to set direction.

In summary, there is no prescriptive model for selecting Product Owners and they may come from either the client side or EY. Tradeoffs may need to be made in selecting them as described below.

Senior candidates

A person with deep experience, moving from a relatively senior management position to a Product Owner role is usually a good candidate, as they will most likely have:

  • A good overview of the business, business strategy, market and customer needs
  • Relationship to key stakeholders
  • Authority to make decisions
  • Well-developed leadership, interpersonal and communication skills

A potential drawback is that such people usually play an important role in the organization, securing sufficient time to play the Product Owner role may not be easy. If this is not possible the individual will need to split time between Product Owner and other responsibilities, potentially neglecting one (or both).

Less senior candidates

If a less senior candidate is chosen, it is more likely that they will be dedicated to the Product Owner role and they may possess relevant business knowledge. However, there are some potential impediments to the individual's effectiveness. In particular:

  • Potentially less insight to market, business strategy and customer needs
  • Less developed senior stakeholder network
  • Lack of authority to make decisions independently, leading to increased decision making time

Golden balance

A good candidate to become a Product Owner, seniority-wise, is the most senior person able to dedicate sufficient time to the project. A senior individual with limited time could be supported in their duties by a business analyst to be an effective Product Owner (e.g., product backlog maintenance). A less senior candidate could be empowered through the support of a senior individual who assists them to make decisions and leverage the necessary stakeholders.
